seoTitle: How to Buy a Domain on GoDaddy Auctions
metaDescription: Learn how to browse, bid on, or buy now on GoDaddy Auctions, plus what to check before you bid and how to complete a secure purchase.
intro: GoDaddy Auctions is where expired, premium, and otherwise unavailable domain names change hands, and it works nothing like grabbing a fresh .com off the standard search page. You're bidding against other buyers, working against a countdown clock, and weighing signals like traffic and backlink authority before you commit money. This guide walks through signing in, reading the Auctions dashboard, and understanding what the numbers next to each listing mean before you place a bid.
costNote: Placing a bid costs nothing beyond what you win the domain for, or a buy-now price if you take that route. Two things are still gated behind account status: bidding on expired or premium ("valued priced") listings needs you to join the GoDaddy Auctions program, and until your account passes bidder verification you're capped at two bids totalling $1,500 combined.

steps.heading: Sign in to your GoDaddy account
steps.body: Go to GoDaddy's sign-in page and enter your username or customer number along with your password. The same account you use for domains, hosting, and email works here; there's no separate Auctions login. You can also sign in with Apple, Facebook, or Google if you originally set your account up that way. The "Keep me signed in on this device" checkbox is worth using if you plan to check auctions regularly, since some listings move fast enough that re-logging in costs you time you don't have.

image.caption: GoDaddy's sign-in screen, with username and password fields and options to sign in with Apple, Facebook, or Google instead.

steps.heading: Open the Auctions dashboard
steps.body: Once signed in, navigate to Auctions, which opens into its own dashboard with a left-hand menu for Search, Watch List, Buying List, and Settings. The main page surfaces two panels right away: "Auctions Ending Soon," which lists domains with a live countdown next to their current price, and "Auctions Added Today," showing what's freshly listed. A prominent Join Auctions button also sits at the top; that's the membership gate covered in the cost note above, separate from just having a standard GoDaddy account.

image.caption: The Auctions dashboard, with Auctions Ending Soon and Auctions Added Today panels listing domains, current prices, and time remaining.

steps.heading: Read the listing columns before you bid
steps.body:
Use Advanced Search or the column headers to sort by Estimated Value, Time Left, or Majestic TF, a third-party trust flow metric that gives a rough sense of a domain's existing backlink authority. A domain with a Majestic TF of 1 or higher has at least some link history, which can matter if you're buying for SEO value and not just the name; a value of 0 means it's starting from scratch in Google's eyes regardless of how good the name sounds.

Opening the full listing adds Bids, Price, Traffic, and Age columns. Bids tells you how contested a listing already is: a domain with dozens of bids and climbing will keep moving, while one with only two might still be gettable near its current price. Traffic and Age are populated for expired-domain auctions specifically, so a blank or N/A in either column on other listing types means no data was tracked, not zero. Age is the domain's registration length in years, which matters because older domains can carry more trust with search engines than a brand-new one, independent of backlinks.

image.caption: Auction results sorted by Estimated Value, with Time Left and Majestic TF columns for judging a domain's existing authority.

steps.heading: Place a bid or buy instantly
steps.body:
GoDaddy Auctions runs on proxy bidding, not a simple "type a number, that's your bid" system. Clicking Place Bid asks for the maximum you're willing to pay; the system then bids only the smallest amount needed to keep you in the lead, and automatically raises your bid step by step as others outbid you, up to that maximum. You're notified if someone eventually outbids your max entirely.

Some listings instead show a fixed Buy Now price, letting you skip bidding and purchase immediately if you don't want to risk losing the domain to a late bid. Buy-now purchases go through GoDaddy's normal cart and checkout. Decide which approach fits the domain before you start: buy-now suits a name you can't afford to lose, bidding suits one you'd like but won't chase past your own ceiling.

image.caption: The full auction listing table with Bids, Price, Traffic, and Age columns next to a Place Bid button for each domain.

steps.heading: Check membership and verification limits before you bid seriously
steps.body: Bidding on expired or premium listings requires joining GoDaddy's Auctions program through the Join Auctions button. Separately, your account's verification status caps how much you can commit: an unverified account is limited to two active bids totalling $1,500 combined, while buy-now or make-offer purchases under that amount don't require verification at all. If you plan to chase something above that ceiling, complete bidder verification before you get attached to a specific domain, not at the moment you try to place the bid.

steps.heading: Complete payment securely once you win
steps.body: Winning a bid or completing a buy-now purchase moves you into GoDaddy's standard checkout, where payment is processed the same way as any other GoDaddy purchase. Domains bought through auction still need to be transferred into your account and, if you want continuity, pointed at your existing hosting or DNS. Budget a little time after the purchase completes for that transfer to finish before the domain is fully usable.

troubleshooting.problem: The price barely moves after placing a bid
troubleshooting.cause: GoDaddy's proxy bidding only raises your bid the minimum amount needed to stay ahead. The number you entered is your ceiling, not the amount that gets shown as the current price.
troubleshooting.fix: Check your maximum in the Buying List instead of assuming the listing price reflects what you offered; it climbs on its own as others bid, until it reaches your cap.

troubleshooting.problem: A bid gets rejected, or you can't place a second one
troubleshooting.cause: Unverified accounts are limited to two active bids totalling $1,500 combined.
troubleshooting.fix: Complete GoDaddy's bidder verification if you want to bid on more auctions at once or commit above that combined total.

troubleshooting.problem: Traffic or Age shows blank on a listing you're interested in
troubleshooting.cause: Those two columns are populated for expired-domain auctions specifically; other auction types don't carry that history.
troubleshooting.fix: Treat a blank field as unknown, not zero, and check traffic independently with a third-party tool if it matters to the purchase.

faq.question: Do I need special membership to bid on GoDaddy Auctions?
faq.answer: Bidding on expired-domain and premium listings needs GoDaddy's Auctions program membership, joined via the Join Auctions button on the dashboard. Buy-now and make-offer purchases under $1,500 don't need it.

faq.question: How does bidding actually work, do I just enter a price?
faq.answer: You enter a maximum bid, not a fixed offer. GoDaddy's proxy bidding system bids the smallest amount necessary to keep you ahead and keeps raising it automatically as others bid, up to your maximum.

faq.question: What does "buy now" mean on an auction listing?
faq.answer: It lets you skip bidding entirely and purchase the domain immediately at a fixed price, instead of risking being outbid before the auction closes.

faq.question: What does Majestic TF mean on a listing?
faq.answer: Majestic Trust Flow is a third-party metric estimating a domain's existing backlink authority. A TF of 0 means little to no link history, while a higher number suggests some established SEO value.

faq.question: Is there a limit on how much I can bid?
faq.answer: Yes, until your account is verified: unverified accounts are capped at two active bids totalling $1,500 combined. Verification removes that cap.

faq.question: Is GoDaddy Auctions good for beginners?
faq.answer: It's accessible for beginners, though reading the Bids, Traffic, and Age columns, and understanding that bids are maximums and not fixed offers, takes a little practice before you can judge whether a listing's price is reasonable.
